abstract:
BackgroundAutism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) frequently co-occur, and both are associated with atypical attention and arousal. Whether these associations arise from shared or distinct processes remains unclear because the conditions are rarely modeled jointly and attention and arousal are rarely measured simultaneously.

MethodsWe analyzed eye-tracking data (gaze position and pupil size) collected during naturalistic video viewing from 2,421 youth (aged 5-22) in the Healthy Brain Network. ASD, ADHD-Inattentive, and ADHD-Hyperactive diagnostic statuses were modeled jointly alongside age and sex.

ResultsAtypical gaze trajectories were uniquely associated with ASD. Basic oculomotor control and orienting after scene cuts and to faces were typical, but autistic participants maintained gaze consistently farther from typical viewing locations and spent less time looking at characters, faces, and mouths. Pupil fluctuations were atypical in both ASD and ADHD-Hyperactivity via distinct routes: reduced pupil synchrony in ASD was largely explained by gaze allocation, whereas in ADHD-Hyperactivity it was gaze-independent and accompanied by faster pupil fluctuations.

ConclusionsASD and ADHD show dissociable signatures during natural viewing: ASD differs in what is looked at rather than when, whereas ADHD-Hyperactivity is characterized by faster-fluctuating arousal.
